extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, government contracting officers, procurement officials, and bidders in federal government contracting
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal standards and principles governing government procurement bids, guaranties, bid withdrawal, bid errors and corrections, performance obligations (including impossibility, acts of God, and divisible work), advance payments, and limitations tied to appropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing and correcting bid errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a bidder seeks to amend a bid for a claimed mistake, the bidder must clearly establish the error by evidence under oath and show that the lead-pencil memorandum (or original estimate) was the basis of the bid; if the error is shown to be fundamental and the bid did not express the real intention of the bidder, reformation may be proper but the corrected bid should include the same percentage of profit on the amount of the error as was calculated in the bid, and nothing more. A bidder may not amend to add items already covered by the original estimate if the original estimate was not shown to be the result of a fundamental error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bidder submitted $40,000 with ~13% profit; correction permitted limited to restoring same profit percentage; could not add a separate item for piles that were already in the original estimate. (C. 165U, July 6, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales by sample and description must both conform
rubrics_metrics.description: When a contract/sale is by both sample and description, the goods delivered must conform to the description as well as to the sample; it is not sufficient that the goods correspond to the sample alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bidder submitted sample labeled 'sperm oil' but delivered fish oil; although conforming to the sample, the oil did not meet the descriptive term 'sperm oil' and the sale failed. (C. £4332, Jan. 14, 1909; 26294, Feb. 28, 1910.) Also applied to 'basting cotton' where standard sample was not known in trade as such. Footnote: cites Uniform Sales Act §14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical or computation errors may void/improvide contract remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: If a bid price results from a clerical mistake or miscalculation (e.g., decimal error) discovered after partial performance, the contract may be not binding on the contractor; remedies include paying for supplies already furnished and re-award to actual lowest bidder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bidder offered to furnish bacon for $23.00 instead of $230 due to clerk carelessness; contract was not binding and supplemental contract awarded; contractor paid only for supplies already delivered. (C. 20323, Sept. 4, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict compliance with place-of-performance terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractor must perform at the place(s) specified in the contract; selection of a point outside the contractual description (even if more convenient) does not comply with contract terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: contract described one terminus 'at or near the mouth of Delta River and Bates Rapids'; selecting a point 75 miles from the mouth did not comply. (C. 12705, Apr. 3, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of site by Government does not oblige contractor to accept new site
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Government changes the site of work after award to a location other than the site described in the contract, the contractor is under no legal obligation to perform at the new site even if it is more advantageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: site moved ~450 feet after contract; contractor not legally required to carry out work on new site. (C. 20300, Aug. 31, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute and unconditional performance obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contractor engages expressly and without condition to perform a specific work or service, he is generally bound by his contract and cannot be excused simply because execution proves difficult or personally beyond his power if performance remains within possible private exertion; the contract is an absolute undertaking where no exceptions are stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and contrasts: contractor who agreed absolutely to furnish potatoes/onions cannot be excused because his own crops were destroyed by hail; contractor agreeing absolutely to supply fresh beef was not excused by destruction of his plant in the 1906 earthquake where contract did not contemplate a particular herd or on-premises slaughtering. (C. 11259, Sept. 21, 1901; C. 19820, June 9, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts of God and impossibility—when excuse is available
rubrics_metrics.description: An act of God that renders literal compliance impossible may excuse performance only when the contract relates to particular goods or methods such that literal compliance is impossible; otherwise the contractor must substantially comply by furnishing other goods 'as nearly as practicable' of the same kind and quality, and the Government should be given an opportunity to accept substantial compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: contract requiring hams cured by a process for 60 days — if act of God prevented that method, contractor must still furnish substantially similar hams or be relieved if Government fails to allow substantial compliance. (C. 15152, Aug. 31, 1903.) By contrast, drought making it impossible to furnish specified 'wild Arizona hay' excused contractor (P. 56259, Oct. 31, 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisible contracts—partial destruction does not automatically excuse remaining work
rubrics_metrics.description: If the work under the contract is divisible and only part was destroyed before performance, and the remaining major part remains intact and is not made more difficult or expensive, the partial destruction will not relieve the contractor from completing the remaining portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ~1/7 of a levee washed out before work began; since the work was divisible and the larger part intact, contractor remained obligated to enlarge the rest. (C. 15923, Feb. 18, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary legal impossibility (injunction) suspends but does not extinguish obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: When impossibility of performance is created by law (e.g., injunction) and is only temporary, the contractor's obligation is suspended during the injunction but not extinguished; the United States is not liable for damages for the suspension during the injunction's continuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: injunction obtained by private lessee against dredging leased submerged lands — obligation suspended; U.S. not liable for damages. (C. 22703, Feb. 5, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Bankruptcy/receivership prior to completion does not automatically relieve contractor
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractor forced into bankruptcy and placed in receivership before the completion date is not relieved from the necessity of completing the contract according to its terms; the Government may decline to receive deliveries after the contractual delivery date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bankruptcy before completion of caps contract — contractor remained obligated; Government could refuse late deliveries. (C. 27968, Mar. 13, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Bids do not constitute binding contract until reduced to writing and signed (War Dept/section 3744)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 3744 R.S. (and related War Department practice), a bid alone is not a contract; a contract is not binding until it is reduced to writing and signed by the contracting parties, so a bidder who withdraws before acceptance cannot be held simply on the basis of the bid itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bidder gave guaranty with bid but withdrew before acceptance; bidder could not be held because no written signed contract existed. (P. 65, 378, July 7, 1894; C. 419, Oct. 3, 1894.) Note: guarantors may be liable under guaranty language even if bidder not personally bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawals before opening or before acceptance under Army/War Dept regs
rubrics_metrics.description: Army Regulations paragraph 548 (1910) and similar provisions allow a bidder to withdraw without prejudice before the time for opening bids; language like 'unread' at opening contemplates returning unread bids to withdrawing bidders; withdrawals may be limited to particular items when bids cover multiple items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bidder wired to withdraw his bid on oats only; regulation's 'unread' applied only to that item and did not prohibit reading other items. (C. 28967, Sept. 12, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of guaranty wording and timing (acceptance within period)
rubrics_metrics.description: The binding effect of a guaranty that accompanies a bid depends on its precise wording and the timing of acceptance; guaranties conditioned on acceptance within a specified period (e.g., 60 days) generally do not bind if the bid is withdrawn before acceptance or if acceptance occurs after the guaranty's period unless the guaranty explicitly keeps the proposal open or differently worded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney General and department interpretations differ; earlier wording often allowed withdrawal before acceptance, leading to later revision of guaranty forms to explicitly keep proposals open for a period and bind sureties if withdrawn. (Card 23180, May 12 & 18, 1908; form example included.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Guaranty requirement may be directory not mandatory — contracting officer discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations requiring guaranties to accompany proposals (e.g., paragraph 533/543 Army Regs) have been held directory in some cases: absence of a guaranty does not necessarily invalidate the contract, though in good faith to other bidders a bid without a guaranty should not be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited where contract was valid despite missing guaranty but practice requires caution. (C. 6285; 7613; 7956; 14535; 20670; 21707.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Guaranty must be present and applicable to department/officer — 'on file' may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A notation that an 'annual guaranty is on file' that applies only to another department (e.g., Navy) does not satisfy a requirement that a guaranty accompany the proposal for the department advertising the procurement; late filing after opening may not cure initial defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Annual guaranty for 1910 on file' referencing Navy Department only; subsequent filing a few days later did not render the bid properly considered. (C. 27062, July 22, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Form attachments that do not expressly require guaranty do not necessarily bar acceptance of unguaranteed bids
rubrics_metrics.description: If specifications attach a form of guaranty but contain no distinct provision requiring a guaranty or stating that unaccompanied proposals will not be received, an unguaranteed bid may be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (C. 21707, Jan. 21, 1907.) Contrast with explicit advertisements/specifications that state no proposal unaccompanied by guaranty will be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certified check may be accepted in lieu of guaranty and treated as substantial compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Where instructions permit or purchasing officers accept a certified check instead of the written guaranty, the check can be treated as a substantive compliance and applied to secure the Government under the terms specified in the instructions; however, the bidder's personal liability beyond the check may be limited if no further signed contract exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bidder submitted certified check 'in lieu' of guaranty and it was applied accordingly (C. 7613, Jan. 26, 1900). But where no written contract existed as required by section 3714, the bidder was not liable beyond the amount of the check (C. 28575, June 21, 1911; 28928, Sept. 6, 1911). Paragraph 543 (A.R. 1910) contemplates certified checks for guaranty amount and return when no longer required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent of certified_check retention may create liability beyond its face value
rubrics_metrics.description: If specifications state that a certified check 'will be retained until the completion of the contract' and the contractor defaults causing re-let at higher cost, the check may be applied to reimburse the Government and suit may be brought for the balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: derrick construction contract with $1,000 certified check retained; contractor failed to commence and Government relet at $2,150 excess — check to be applied and suit for remainder. (C. 15966, Feb. 26, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirements for guaranty-triggered obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where guarantors undertake that bidder will 'within 10 days after being notified of such acceptance enter into a contract' and give bond, actual notice to the bidder is required to trigger the guaranty period; where notice is given by mail, the 10-day period runs from the date the bidder actually received the notice (though receipt raises a presumption of actual notice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guaranties conditioned on a time period expire if acceptance occurs after that period
rubrics_metrics.description: If guaranties accompanying proposals are conditioned on acceptance within a specified period (e.g., 60 days), acceptance after expiration of that period does not make guaranties enforceable unless the bidders are willing to enter into the contracts; guaranties cannot be enforced against unwilling bidders after expiration of the conditional period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proposals for four works — acceptances recommended after guaranty period had expired; acceptances legally permissible but guaranties could not be enforced if bidders declined to enter into contracts. (C. 371, Sept. 22, 1894.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary may require guaranty and blanket/general guaranty may be acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statute absolutely requiring a guaranty with every bid, but under statutes authorizing the Secretary of War to prescribe rules, the Secretary may require guaranties; a properly worded 'blanket' or 'general' guaranty covering all bids by a bidder during the fiscal year could be accepted under regulations, though practical objections exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of deposit/guaranty funds when contractor defaults
rubrics_metrics.description: Money deposited as guaranty for faithful performance may be held in trust and applied to the completion of the contract; after completion as economically as possible the remainder, if any, should be returned to the contractor rather than being forfeited to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: successful bidder deposited $225; after contractor defaulted and work completed, remainder to be returned. (C. 29276, Dec. 2, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on advance of public money (Section 3048) with narrow exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3048 R.S. forbids any advance of public money; payment shall not exceed the value of the service rendered or articles delivered previously to such payment. However, payment of rent in advance for lands leased by the Government where the lessor places the Government in possession is not a violation of section 3048.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (C. 21506, Mar. 17 & July 23, 1908; XII Comp. Dec. 782.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of contracts by appropriations (Section 3679)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3679 R.S. provides that no department shall expend in any one fiscal year sums in excess of appropriations for that year; contracts that bind the Government to future payments in excess of current-year appropriations are unauthorized and unenforceable to the extent they create such future obligations. Military contracts/leases founded on annual appropriations generally bind the Government only for the fiscal year and should, where practicable, run concurrently with the fiscal year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: leases or contracts purporting to bind the Government beyond the fiscal year are inoperative unless specially authorized by statute; leases for 'one year and thereafter until terminated' are problematic if funded from annual appropriations. (R. 31, 40, Nov. 11, 1870; Hooe v. U.S., 218 U.S. 322 cited.)
